text:
Two delivery services both average thirty minutes. One always arrives between twenty-eight and thirty-two. The other swings from five minutes to fifty-five. Same center, completely different experience. What differs is the spread. To measure it, take each delivery's distance from the mean. For the steady service, they run from minus two to plus two, and they cancel out to zero. So square them first. Now they add up to twelve. Divide by nine, one less than the count, and that's the variance. Its square root, back in minutes, is the standard deviation... about one point two. For the erratic service, it's almost eighteen.

So why nine, and not ten? Because the distances are measured from the sample's own mean. And that mean sits closer to its own points than any other number does. These five values come from a population whose true mean is zero. Measure from the truth instead, and the squares grow. So around the sample's mean, the squares run small. Divide by n, and you'd underestimate the spread. Over four thousand samples of five, dividing by n comes out about twenty percent low. Dividing by n minus one lands on the truth. That's why numpy and pandas disagree. numpy divides by n unless you ask, and pandas by n minus one. Squares have one more weakness. A single wild value can swamp them.

Take ten incomes. Nine fall between thirty-eight and a hundred and twenty. The tenth is nine thousand. The standard deviation leaps to over two thousand eight hundred. The interquartile range only measures the middle half, from the first quartile to the third. It's fourteen, whatever the top earner makes. Its cousin, the median absolute deviation, takes the typical distance from the median. Here, eight. So pair them. A mean goes with a standard deviation, and a median goes with the IQR. Still, a center and a spread can't tell you what the data looks like.
